content_metadata.description: This video explores the celestial phenomena behind the changing North Star, focusing on Earth's precession and its effects.

qAndA.question: What color is the nebula shown in the video?

qAndA.answer: The interaction of its equatorial bulge with the gravitational forces of the Sun and Moon.
qAndA.question: What causes the Earth's wobble?
Besides Polaris, what other stars are mentioned as future North Stars?

qAndA.answer: Polaris was at its closest point to the North Celestial Pole in 2017.

qAndA.answer: The video evokes a sense of awe and wonder, highlighting the constant movement and change occurring in the universe over vast timescales, prompting reflection on our place within this grand cosmic dance.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Everyone knows that Polaris is the North Star, but did you know that this will actually change?
In just 5,470 years, this star, Al-Darrimen, will be the North Star, and in about 13,000 years,
it will have changed again to the super bright star Vega.
So why does the North Star change over time?
The main reason is that Earth is not quite spherical.
It's actually slightly wider at the equator than it is at the poles.
And this equatorial bulge interacts with the sun and moon's gravity to give the spinning Earth a little wobble that we call procession.
The whole processional cycle for the Earth takes about 26,000 years, and in that time, many different stars will be the ones closest to the North Celestial pole.
And whichever one is closest at any given time is what we call the North Star.
Polaris was closest to the North Celestial pole in 2017, but now is getting further and further away from it every day.

youtube_description: Everyone knows that Polaris, is the North Star, but did you know that this will actually CHANGE? In just 5,470 years, this star, Al Dare a min will be the North Star, and in about 13,000 years, it will have changed again to the super bright star Vega. So why does the North Star change over time? The main reason is that Earth is not quite spherical. It is just slightly wider at the equator than it is at the poles and this equatorial bulge interacts with the sun and moon’s gravity to give the spinning earth a slow wobble that we call precession. The whole precessional cycle for the earth takes about 26,000 years and in that time many different stars will be the ones closest to the north celestial pole, whichever one is closest at any given time is what we call the north star. Polaris was closest to the north celestial pole in 2017, but now is getting further and further away from it every day, but will still be the North Star for many years to come.
